questions.prompt: Predict which edits affect the original draft, then explain the difference between an immutable binding, a value copy, and shared reference identity.
questions.scenario: A synthetic Selection struct stores var specialtyID: Int64? and let notes: Notes, where Notes is a mutable class. original is let-bound; edited is a var-bound copy. You assign edited.specialtyID = 20 and edited.notes.text = "Changed".
questions.androidBridge: Kotlin val and Swift let both constrain reassignment, but a Kotlin mutable data-class assignment aliases an object while Swift struct assignment gives value semantics. Kotlin data-class copy is also shallow for nested references; neither copy recursively clones mutable objects.
rubric: Predicts independent specialtyID values but shared notes.text.
Explains why original.specialtyID cannot be assigned through a let-bound struct.
Distinguishes equality from class identity checked with ===.
Describes array value semantics without promising immediate physical copying.
questions.answerHTML:
Changing edited.specialtyID changes only the copied struct value. The original keeps its earlier identifier. A let binding prevents replacing or mutating stored parts of that struct through the binding. It does not recursively freeze every reachable object: both structs hold the same Notes reference, so changing that object's text is visible through both.

Use === to compare class identity; == expresses equality when the type supplies the appropriate conformance. Swift arrays also have observable value semantics, although their storage may be shared until mutation requires separation. That implementation does not imply recursive cloning of elements that are classes. For an independently editable draft, use value fields throughout the mutable domain or explicitly copy the referenced data. State the required independence before choosing the representation.
followUps: What changes if edited is also bound with let?
What does copying an array of Notes objects preserve and what remains shared?
pitfalls: Claiming that a struct copy deep-copies its entire object graph.
Treating let as a guarantee that every reachable property is immutable.

questions.prompt: Repair an absence-handling boundary without turning missing procedure IDs or empty names into stored sentinel values.
questions.scenario: A synthetic form stores procedureID as Int64? and patientName as String?. Its renderer uses patientName ?? "Unknown", while submission force-unwraps procedureID. A teammate proposes storing -1 and treating an empty name as nil.
questions.androidBridge: Kotlin nullable values and Swift optionals both represent absence. Kotlin's Elvis operator resembles ??, but neither operator validates a present empty string; Swift guard let introduces a nonoptional binding whose failure branch must leave the scope.
rubric: Separates nil, an empty present string, and a display fallback.
Uses guard let with a deliberate return or error for missing procedure.
Keeps output-only fallback values out of the domain model.
Explains why optional chaining does not validate present contents.
questions.answerHTML:
The name renderer substitutes Unknown only when the optional is nil. A present empty string remains empty. Whether blank text is acceptable is a validation rule that must be stated separately; optional unwrapping cannot decide it. Preserve absence in the model instead of introducing an identifier such as -1 that downstream code might mistake for a real value.

At submission, use guard let procedure = draft.procedureID else { return }, with the failure branch presenting the agreed selection requirement or returning a typed failure. After the guard, procedure is nonoptional. A force unwrap instead traps if the assumption is violated. Test missing and present identifiers, plus nil, empty, and nonempty names. Optional chaining skips access when its receiver is absent; it still permits invalid present content. Display defaults should explain a state without silently changing the submitted data.
followUps: How would you represent whitespace-only input if the product rejects it?
When is an optional return preferable to a thrown validation error?
pitfalls: Assuming ?? replaces empty strings.
Using force unwraps because current fixtures contain an ID.

questions.prompt: Explain why search results use associated values while a wire reason code can use raw values, and show how an exhaustive renderer extracts its payload.
questions.scenario: A synthetic SearchState has idle, loading, loaded(providers: [String]), and failed(message: String). A separate CancellationReason has fixed String identifiers supplied to a service.
questions.androidBridge: A Kotlin sealed hierarchy with payload-bearing subtypes resembles a Swift associated-value enum. Kotlin when smart-casts a subtype; Swift switch binds case payloads directly. Raw-value enums represent fixed case identifiers rather than per-instance sealed-state data.
rubric: Distinguishes instance payloads from fixed raw identifiers.
Uses case let .loaded(names) to bind the array.
Explains exhaustive coverage and the benefit of omitting default for these local states.
Handles an unknown raw string as a failable conversion rather than force-unwrapping.
questions.answerHTML:
An associated value belongs to a particular enum instance. Two .loaded values can contain different provider arrays, and .failed carries the message for that failure. A raw-value enum instead maps each declared case to a fixed identifier. It cannot use a raw string as a substitute for an arbitrary result payload.

Render with an exhaustive switch. The branch case let .loaded(names) extracts the array into a local immutable binding; it does not cast a subclass. Handle its empty array as successful no matches, and give idle, loading, and failure their own behavior. Adding a case then exposes missing decisions at the switches that need updating. Converting an unrecognized service string with a raw-value initializer yields nil; the boundary must choose a deliberate fallback or rejection. The enum describes possible states, while transition rules still require implementation and tests.
followUps: When does if case fit better than an exhaustive switch?
Would making SearchState optional add a useful state to this renderer?
pitfalls: Calling rawValue the payload of every enum instance.
Using a broad default that hides a newly introduced product state.

questions.prompt: Replace contradictory search flags with a state model, then decide whether offline deserves a distinct case or a typed failure payload.
questions.scenario: A synthetic screen can currently hold isLoading = true, hasError = true, and providers = []. Product behavior should distinguish not searched, in progress, successful no matches, and retryable failure; offline may retain old content.
questions.androidBridge: Android sealed UI state can replace unrelated LiveData or StateFlow flags, just as Swift enum cases constrain combinations. Neither StateFlow nor an enum enforces legal transitions, cancellation, or retention of prior content by itself.
rubric: Models idle, loading, empty success, and failure as distinct states.
Connects offline representation to its specific user action and content policy.
Explains which contradictory combinations construction prevents.
Defines transition tests rather than claiming exhaustiveness proves workflow correctness.
questions.answerHTML:
Start with idle, loading, loaded(providers:), and failed. Constructing one case prevents the screen from independently declaring loading and failure at the same time. An empty array inside loaded means a completed successful search, so it offers another search rather than implying that the user should retry a failed operation.

Add an offline case when it owns meaningfully different behavior, such as a connection explanation and retained previous results. Otherwise a typed reason inside failed can express the distinction without duplicating presentation. If prior content is retained, make that payload and its freshness explicit rather than leaving a hidden array beside the state. Specify start, completion, retry, and replacement transitions and test their visible outcomes. Exhaustive switching forces rendering decisions but cannot decide whether a transition is legal or whether the displayed data belongs to the current request.
followUps: How would loading with retained previous content change the payload?
Which test would distinguish idle from loaded([])?
pitfalls: Collapsing successful no matches into a retryable error.
Assuming the compiler validates the complete transition policy.

questions.prompt: Predict calls through concrete and protocol-typed values when badge() is declared only in an extension, then repair the contract if specialization is required.
questions.scenario: BadgeNaming has no requirements. Its extension defines badge() returning "default". FeaturedBadge conforms and defines badge() returning "featured". Calls are made on FeaturedBadge and on any BadgeNaming holding that value.
questions.androidBridge: Kotlin extension functions are statically selected and provide a useful analogy for Swift extension-only helpers. A Swift protocol requirement with a default implementation participates in protocol dispatch; a Kotlin extension cannot retroactively add interface conformance.
rubric: Predicts featured through the concrete value and default through the existential.
Distinguishes extension-only methods from protocol requirements.
Moves badge() into the protocol when polymorphic specialization is promised.
Explains that any hides the concrete conformer without requiring it to be a class.
questions.answerHTML:
The concrete call selects FeaturedBadge.badge() and returns featured. Through any BadgeNaming, the call selects the extension-only helper and returns default. The helper was never declared as a protocol requirement, so the conformer's same-named method does not fulfill a polymorphic promise at that boundary.

If callers require specialized behavior through the protocol, declare func badge() -> String inside BadgeNaming. The extension can still provide the default implementation, and the conformer supplies its own implementation for the requirement. An existential holds a conforming value while hiding its concrete type; structs as well as classes can conform. Test the same behavior through the boundary consumers actually use. Testing only the concrete type can miss this discrepancy. Extensions can add methods and computed properties, but cannot introduce stored instance properties to keep hidden badge state.
followUps: When is an extension-only helper an intentional design?
Why can a concrete-only fake test pass while a protocol consumer behaves differently?
pitfalls: Calling every same-named method an override.
Assuming any Protocol implies reference semantics.

questions.prompt: Explain why a service consumer loses retry behavior with try?, and identify the separate contract change needed when it starts storing its success callback.
questions.scenario: A synchronous synthetic appointment consumer evaluates (try? service.appointments()) ?? [] and invokes onSuccess. A later revision saves onSuccess in a handler for invocation after the function returns.
questions.androidBridge: Kotlin runCatching followed by getOrDefault(emptyList()) can erase failures like Swift try? followed by ?? []. Kotlin callbacks have no direct @escaping counterpart: Swift uses the annotation to permit a plain closure parameter to outlive its call, without specifying a thread or dispatcher.
rubric: Identifies offline and empty success as the outcomes being merged.
Replaces fallback with explicit propagation or do/catch and distinct callbacks.
Requires @escaping when the plain callback parameter is stored.
Separates escaping from asynchronous execution, capture ownership, and guaranteed invocation.
questions.answerHTML:
try? discards the thrown error and returns nil for failure. The following empty-array fallback makes offline indistinguishable from a successful response containing no appointments. The compiler accepts this, but the consumer loses the information needed to offer retry. Use do/catch with separate success and failure paths, or propagate the error to an owner that can map it deliberately. Successful empty data must still take the success path.

The original synchronous callbacks need no escaping annotation because they run before the consumer returns. Once the plain callback parameter is stored, mark that parameter @escaping and review the retaining handler and captured objects. Escaping permits a longer lifetime; it establishes neither background execution nor weak capture. Define how often completion can occur and when the handler releases the callback. Test nonempty success, empty success, and offline independently, including cleanup when delayed work is abandoned.
followUps: When would deliberately using try? preserve the intended domain meaning?
What ownership graph would you draw if the stored callback captured its handler?
pitfalls: Using empty success as a universal recovery value.
Treating @escaping as a background-thread or memory-safety annotation.

questions.prompt: Draw the stored-callback ownership cycle and explain why clearing it in deinit cannot repair the cycle.
questions.scenario: A synthetic Screen owns tapCallback; that closure uses self.name. After the external screen variable is set to nil, a weak probe remains nonnil. Another variable also holds a saved copy of the callback.
questions.androidBridge: JVM tracing garbage collection can reclaim an unreachable object cycle. Swift ARC releases objects when strong ownership ends, so an unreachable strong cycle can persist. A Java WeakReference analogy does not reproduce Swift weak references' automatically nil optional access.
rubric: Draws Screen to closure and closure to Screen as strong edges.
Explains why dropping one external owner leaves the cycle.
Explains why deinit cannot run to break a cycle that prevents deallocation.
Shows how weak capture permits a saved callback to outlive the screen safely.
questions.answerHTML:
The screen strongly owns its stored closure, and the closure strongly captures the screen. Setting the external variable to nil removes only that variable's edge. The two internal strong edges still retain each other, so ARC cannot release the screen. Cleanup placed exclusively in deinit is unreachable while those owners prevent deallocation.

For a callback that should tolerate the screen disappearing, use [weak self] and an absent-owner branch such as guard let self else { return }. A saved callback then owns the closure without owning the screen through that capture. Optional invocation handles a missing callback; the guard handles a present callback whose screen has gone. The unwrapped local self temporarily provides strong ownership during its use. Verify the controlled graph with a weak probe after removing known strong owners. Deallocation observations support this experiment without promising exact source-line timing under every optimization setting.
followUps: When is strong capture appropriate for required work?
Why is unowned unsafe if the saved callback can run after screen release?
pitfalls: Assuming ARC discovers unreachable cycles like a tracing collector.
Putting the only cycle-breaking operation inside deinit.

questions.prompt: Audit a nested closure after weak self is promoted, and choose a lifetime policy for queued work that may outlive a dismissed screen.
questions.scenario: Screen owns a queue of callbacks. An outer [weak self] callback performs guard let self, then stores an inner closure on that queue which uses self. The inner work can remain queued indefinitely.
questions.androidBridge: Kotlin coroutine or callback captures can also retain a screen beyond its intended lifecycle. Lifecycle cancellation is a separate policy in both systems; Swift's outer weak capture does not automatically apply to a nested closure, and ARC cycles differ from JVM reachability collection.
rubric: Labels the inner closure's capture of the promoted self as strong.
Identifies the possible Screen to queue to closure to Screen cycle.
Distinguishes bounded operation retention from indefinite retention.
Selects weak screen updates or a dedicated operation owner according to required behavior.
questions.answerHTML:
The outer weak capture changes only that closure's edge. After guard let self, the body has a strong local reference. An inner stored closure using that binding can capture it strongly, creating screen-to-queue-to-closure-to-screen ownership. The outer annotation does not propagate a weak policy into nested work.

Decide whether the queued operation belongs to the screen. If its only purpose is updating a visible screen, give the inner callback its own weak capture and define removal or cancellation when the flow ends. If a save must finish after dismissal, a dedicated operation owner can retain the service and data it needs, while treating screen updates separately. Strong retention until a reliable completion and release path is bounded ownership; work queued indefinitely lacks that assurance. Inspect completion, cancellation, and queue clearing, then use a controlled pending callback to test release. Replacing weak with unowned would substitute a lifetime assumption and possible trap for an ownership policy.
followUps: How would you prove that an apparently long retention has a bounded release path?
What changes if the inner closure captures a copied String rather than self?
pitfalls: Assuming weak capture is inherited by every nested callback.
Using unowned because work usually completes quickly.

questions.prompt: Explain the build axes needed to interpret a Swift package inside a generated iOS workspace without treating every version number as the same setting.
questions.scenario: A synthetic package declares tools 5.9 and minimum iOS 17. A newer installed compiler builds it; a neighboring target explicitly selects Swift 6 language mode. The learner asks which setting determines API availability and which determines source checking.
questions.androidBridge: A Gradle module resembles a build target, and build types or flavors help reason about configurations. An Xcode scheme plans actions across targets rather than defining a flavor; Swift tools version, language mode, SDK, and deployment target are separate axes just as Gradle, Kotlin compiler, and Android SDK settings are distinct.
rubric: Separates installed compiler, manifest tools version, language mode, SDK, and deployment target.
Defines target, scheme, configuration, and destination distinctly.
Does not infer one target's language mode from its neighbor.
Explains that SDK API presence does not ensure support on the minimum runtime.
questions.answerHTML:
The installed compiler is the implementation performing compilation. The package tools declaration specifies the minimum tooling and manifest API level; it also affects defaults, but is not simply the installed compiler number. The effective language mode controls source compatibility and checking. Inspect the selected target's actual settings rather than borrowing a neighboring target's explicit mode.

The SDK supplies compile-time platform APIs, while the deployment target states the oldest supported runtime. An API present in the SDK may still need availability handling for that runtime. A target defines a component, its sources, dependencies, and output. A configuration supplies build settings; a scheme plans actions using targets; a destination selects where an action runs. Record all of these when diagnosing a build. A SwiftPM product exposes targets to consumers, and its product or package name need not equal the imported module name.
followUps: What evidence would establish the failing target's effective language mode?
Why can a package export multiple products without creating one import name for the entire package?
pitfalls: Equating a newer compiler with Swift 6 mode in every target.
Treating the deployment target as the SDK or tools version.

questions.prompt: Choose the next diagnostic and smallest meaningful verification for a missing module, a UIKit host import failure, and tests that compile but are never discovered.
questions.scenario: A synthetic FoundationLab package runs on the host. A learner adds a UIKit-dependent test, sees a missing-module error elsewhere, and finds no executed tests in a generated workspace. They propose regenerating everything and disabling signing.
questions.androidBridge: Gradle dependency graphs, source sets, test tasks, and test runners provide useful diagnostic categories. SwiftPM host tests and Xcode destination-based tests have different platform contracts; an Xcode scheme's test action is not an Android variant, and generic signing changes do not resolve module discovery.
rubric: Checks dependency and product exposure for the actual missing module.
Checks platform and destination for the UIKit import.
Checks test source membership, framework discovery, and scheme test action.
States the evidence scope of standalone compilation, swift test, and an app-hosted run.
questions.answerHTML:
Classify the first actionable diagnostic before changing the graph. A missing module suggests inspecting the consuming target's dependency, the exported product and module name, source membership, and supported platform. A UIKit import in a host-only test suggests the chosen platform is wrong for that test; use an appropriate iOS target and destination or keep the pure model test independent of UIKit.

Compilation without executed tests requires checking the test target's source glob, framework discovery conventions, and the selected scheme's test action. Listing a workspace verifies structure, not that it builds or runs. Keep the pure model lab on swift test for fast behavioral feedback and use Xcode for platform integration. Record the selected toolchain, target, configuration, and destination with results. Regenerating or changing signing without a related diagnostic can obscure the cause. A passing package test validates that package's behavior, not navigation, signing, or a full application.
followUps: What changes if the missing module is a product name rather than a target name?
Which artifact would demonstrate that a discovered test actually executed?
pitfalls: Calling every failure an Xcode problem without checking the failing boundary.
Reporting host tests as evidence of successful iOS app integration.

questions.prompt: Describe a small load boundary and its meaningful tests for the FoundationLab search core, including a proof that validation prevents the service call.
questions.scenario: SearchDraft contains optional specialty and procedure IDs plus a query. Missing specialty blocks search; missing procedure is allowed. The injected synchronous service can return names, return [], or throw offline.
questions.androidBridge: A Kotlin interface and deterministic fake are analogous to a Swift protocol and fake. Swift struct drafts have value semantics unlike assignment of mutable Kotlin data-class objects; Swift Testing @Test and #expect are not JUnit annotations or assertions despite similar behavioral roles.
rubric: Validates specialty before invoking the injected service.
Maps [] to loaded and offline to a distinct failure.
Uses a spy or controlled fake to assert no service call for missing specialty.
Tests copy independence and display fallback without claiming UI coverage.
questions.answerHTML:
Make load(draft:service:) return a state enum. First guard that specialty exists; on failure, return the selection-required state before invoking the service. Inside do/catch, map every successful array, including an empty one, to loaded. Map known offline failure to retry guidance and keep unexpected failure deliberate. Missing procedure remains valid input rather than becoming a sentinel.

Use a deterministic fake configured with a result and a spy that records calls. A validation test should assert both the failure state and zero service calls; merely observing the message does not prove the ordering. Separate tests check independent draft edits, the empty-query display rule, empty success versus offline, and nonempty result preservation. Use Swift Testing or XCTest consistently within each test. These synchronous host tests establish the model boundary's behavior. They do not establish cancellation, localization, rendering, or any real network behavior that the lab does not implement.
followUps: Why does a full-state assertion protect more than a count assertion here?
Which additional requirement would whitespace-only query normalization introduce?
pitfalls: Testing only happy-path names and missing offline semantics.
Inferring service-call ordering from a final message alone.

questions.prompt: Assess whether the lab tests protect behavior when a deliberate mutation replaces do/catch with a try?-to-empty fallback.
questions.scenario: A synthetic lab mutation returns loaded((try? service.search(for: draft)) ?? []). The suite still passes because it checks only that results contain zero elements for both offline and no matches.
questions.androidBridge: Kotlin tests that assert list size after runCatching.getOrDefault(emptyList()) have the same blind spot. Swift enum equality compares the represented state when Equatable conformance is available; this is a behavioral assertion, not a guarantee supplied by the test framework itself.
rubric: Explains the exact offline-to-empty transformation.
Replaces count-only assertions with expected terminal states.
Uses the deliberate mutation to demonstrate a test's sensitivity.
Names an unimplemented concern that passing model tests cannot establish.
questions.answerHTML:
The mutation preserves the count while changing the outcome. Offline now becomes loaded([]), so a zero-count assertion cannot distinguish it from successful no matches. Add an assertion that the empty-success fixture yields loaded with an empty array and that the offline fixture yields the agreed failed state. Assert the states differ, using suitable equality or case matching.

Run the deliberate mutation against those expectations: the offline assertion should fail for the lost retry behavior. Restore explicit error mapping after inspecting that failure. This checks that the test detects a product distinction rather than reproducing private branch structure. Keep fixtures deterministic and independent of real requests. A passing suite still leaves requirements such as whitespace normalization, localized messages, and later asynchronous cancellation unverified. If callbacks are introduced, their lifetime and captures need a fresh review. Neither the mutation exercise nor reading its worked solution establishes the learner's own execution results.
followUps: Which mutation would expose a missing specialty-validation test?
How would you retain typed failures if a message string becomes too weak a contract?
pitfalls: Changing expected output until the deliberately broken implementation passes.
Counting a compiler success as test execution.

questions.prompt: Walk through the review owner's empty success, offline failure, and saved callback after release, connecting state representation to ownership.
questions.scenario: A synthetic ReviewOwner stores a refresh callback capturing weak self and consumes a throwing protocol service. A saved copy refreshes the owner, the external owner variable is cleared, and the saved callback is invoked again.
questions.androidBridge: Android sealed outcomes and an injected interface support the same separation of empty success from failure. Kotlin callback storage can retain an owner, but JVM garbage collection and Swift ARC have different cycle behavior; weak capture does not implement a LifecycleOwner-style stop policy.
rubric: Predicts loaded([]) as no matches and offline as retry.
Explains the saved closure's lifetime separately from the owner's lifetime.
Explains guard let self and the harmless absent-owner path.
Distinguishes safe memory access from whether a still-alive screen should accept an update.
questions.answerHTML:
The first callback unwraps its weak owner and invokes the service. Successful empty data becomes loaded with an empty payload, which the exhaustive summary renders as no matches. Offline follows the error path and renders retry. These states remain distinct even though neither displays provider names.

The saved variable strongly owns the closure, but the closure's weak capture does not own ReviewOwner. Once every other strong owner is removed, the weak probe can become nil. Calling the saved closure then reaches its absent-owner guard and returns safely. The local self created by successful unwrapping temporarily owns the instance during use. Because the initializer constructs a stored closure directly, there is no incoming plain closure parameter requiring an escaping annotation. Finally, ownership safety does not establish lifecycle correctness: an owner retained elsewhere may still be alive after its flow ends, so asynchronous extensions would need an explicit update and cancellation policy.
followUps: What annotation changes if the initializer accepts and stores a plain callback parameter?
How would a nested stored callback alter the ownership graph?
pitfalls: Assuming the saved closure must keep its weak owner alive.
Treating successful optional unwrapping as permission to update any screen lifecycle state.

questions.prompt: Turn three review findings into distinct, evidence-backed diagnostic plans instead of prescribing one broad build change.
questions.scenario: A synthetic walkthrough finds a protocol conformance error, an unavailable imported module, and a compiling test target with no run result. A reviewer points to the installed compiler version as the explanation for all three.
questions.androidBridge: Android signature checking, Gradle module resolution, and JUnit discovery are separate diagnostic boundaries too. Swift tools declarations and Xcode scheme actions have their own roles; a Kotlin compiler or Gradle version analogy does not determine another Swift target's effective language mode.
rubric: Checks labels, parameter types, return types, and effects for conformance.
Checks dependency, platform, and source membership for module resolution.
Checks test conventions and selected test action for execution.
Separates source observation, predicted behavior, and retained execution evidence.
questions.answerHTML:
For conformance, compare the protocol requirement and implementation: operation name, argument labels, parameter and return types, and throwing or asynchronous effects. For an unavailable module, inspect the consuming target, exposed product, import name, dependency edge, and platform. For compiling but unexecuted tests, inspect target inclusion, framework discovery, and the scheme's test action, then look for an actual run artifact.

The installed compiler alone cannot settle any of those questions. Its version differs from manifest tools requirements, effective language mode, SDK, and deployment target. Write the selected build route beside each finding. In the walkthrough, keep source-visible facts separate from predicted consequences and checks you have executed. A verified source glob supports membership; a test result supports execution; an isolated program supports only its own language and ownership behavior. A useful handoff names the narrow next check and its expected evidence rather than promising that regeneration will fix every category.
followUps: Which evidence would distinguish an async requirement mismatch from a module problem?
How would you report a source-observed ownership risk before reproducing it?
pitfalls: Borrowing build settings from a neighboring target.
Calling a test file in the repository a passing test result.

questions.prompt: Explain why a counter survives a push-and-pop return and why disappearance does not prove deallocation or terminal cancellation.
questions.scenario: A synthetic UIKit counter reaches two, pushes a detail controller, and later becomes visible again. Diagnostic callbacks show one initial view load and repeated appearance events. It may also be covered by a presentation.
questions.androidBridge: Android Activity and Fragment callbacks used from Kotlin or Java help separate setup from repeated visibility. UIKit controller ownership, view loading, containment, and scene activity are distinct mechanisms; viewDidDisappear is not an exact onDestroy or terminal onStop equivalent.
rubric: Explains navigation-stack retention of the existing counter controller.
Separates initialization, view loading, appearance, layout, and deallocation.
Assigns one-time hierarchy setup without resetting state on every appearance.
Requires removal or dismissal evidence before reporting a terminal outcome.
questions.answerHTML:
The navigation stack retains the existing counter controller while detail is shown. Its stored count remains two because returning reveals the same owner; it does not necessarily create a new controller or reload the hierarchy. Configure one-time view construction in the appropriate loading path, and give repeated appearance-driven refresh a separate product policy.

Controller initialization, view loading, appearance, layout, scene activity, and deallocation describe different events. Accessing the view can load it without making it visible. Layout and appearance callbacks can repeat. Disappearance can mean coverage, a transition, or removal, so it does not by itself justify reporting cancellation. Inspect the navigation or presentation event that ends the flow. A popped controller may still have another strong owner, and a retaining task may delay deallocation. Use deinit as lifetime evidence after auditing owners, while performing timely cleanup at the explicit stopping event required by the feature.
followUps: Where should constraints be installed to avoid duplicate activation on return?
What additional evidence would establish that a pushed controller was removed?
pitfalls: Resetting stored model state on every appearance.
Equating viewDidDisappear with deinit or scene backgrounding.

questions.prompt: Repair the ownership and containment plan for a hosted SwiftUI child whose view was inserted directly into a UIKit parent.
questions.scenario: A synthetic parent calls addSubview(host.view) and retains host in a property. It later removes the view but leaves the property and controller relationship policy unspecified. Layout and appearance behavior are inconsistent.
questions.androidBridge: Adding an Android View is not equivalent to attaching a Fragment with its manager and lifecycle. Similarly, adding UIHostingController.view establishes only a view relationship; UIKit child-controller containment needs its own notifications and ownership, beyond any ComposeView analogy.
rubric: Specifies addChild, view insertion and constraints, then didMove(toParent:).
Specifies willMove(toParent: nil), view removal, and removeFromParent for teardown.
Clears separately owned references and constraints according to the parent's policy.
Explains why view insertion alone omits controller containment.
questions.answerHTML:
A UIHostingController is a controller as well as a source of a view. Adding its root view alone does not establish the controller tree UIKit uses for appearance and other system behavior. In a main-actor UI context, call parent.addChild(host), insert and constrain the view, then call host.didMove(toParent: parent). The incoming willMove notification is handled by addChild.

For removal, call host.willMove(toParent: nil), remove the root view and any separately managed constraints, then host.removeFromParent(). Clear the parent's separate property when its ownership should end; otherwise the child can remain retained even after proper removal. Investigate the actual hierarchy and callback sequence rather than attributing every symptom to SwiftUI rendering. Verify both re-embedding and teardown in a scratch target. This plan explains containment and lifetime, but does not claim a particular appearance failure has been reproduced on a device.
followUps: Who owns the hosted controller returned by a factory that leaves containment to its caller?
Which remaining references would you inspect if a weak probe stays nonnil after removal?
pitfalls: Calling addSubview a complete child-controller attachment.
Expecting view removal to clear a separate strong property automatically.

questions.prompt: Assign State, Binding, Bindable, and plain properties to a shared observable draft, explaining what each provides and what remains outside its contract.
questions.scenario: An iOS 17+ synthetic root creates an @Observable draft. A child edits its name with TextField and another child displays canContinue. The draft is isolated to MainActor and should survive unrelated root updates.
questions.androidBridge: Compose remembered state and state hoisting are useful analogies for SwiftUI identity-associated State and passed bindings. SwiftUI View values are descriptions rather than retained Android View objects; Observation tracks property reads and does not equal StateFlow, persistence, or a ViewModel lifetime.
rubric: Uses root State to preserve the locally owned model reference across stable identity.
Uses Bindable for an observable child's projected editing bindings.
Allows a read-only child to observe through a plain model property.
Separates observation, MainActor isolation, ownership, and persistence.
questions.answerHTML:
The root keeps its locally created observable model in @State, which associates storage with the root's SwiftUI identity. Recreating the View description therefore need not recreate the effective draft. An editing child uses @Bindable when controls require projections such as $draft.name. A Binding provides read and write access to somebody else's source of truth rather than independently storing a second draft.

A read-only child can receive a plain model property and read name or computed canContinue in its body. Observation tracks those property dependencies; it does not require that child to own the model. @MainActor separately defines the mutation domain. Neither annotation persists the draft, restores a process, or defines logout cleanup. Keeping identity stable preserves local state, while intentionally replacing identity can reset it. These examples require supported Observation integration and do not replace the older ObservableObject wrappers used by other lesson examples.
followUps: Why does a computed canContinue avoid a second synchronized validity flag?
What would change for an externally owned legacy ObservableObject?
pitfalls: Using Bindable as a declaration of model ownership or persistence.
Assuming @Observable makes arbitrary concurrent mutation safe.

questions.prompt: Explain a draft initialized from record A that remains after the parent supplies record B, and choose a reset policy that protects unsaved edits.
questions.scenario: A synthetic editor seeds State from an initializer argument. Its identity remains stable when the parent changes the record. A proposed fix attaches a newly generated UUID on every body evaluation, which starts erasing typing.
questions.androidBridge: Compose remember(initialInput) keys can help reason about deliberate resets, but SwiftUI uses its own hierarchy and explicit identity rules. Neither remembered state nor State automatically follows every changed constructor argument or survives process death without a separate restoration mechanism.
rubric: Explains initialization as seeding state for a new identity.
Identifies random changing identity as a cause of repeated resets.
Chooses explicit replacement, record-based identity, or parent ownership with an unsaved-edit policy.
Tests unrelated redraw, record switch, and deliberate reset separately.
questions.answerHTML:
The initializer supplies an initial value when storage is created for an identity. A changed parent input does not necessarily overwrite existing State for the same identity. That behavior can preserve unsaved edits, but here it can also leave record A's draft visible while the parent expects B. Inspect identity and model ownership before assuming observation failed.

Choose an explicit contract: have the parent own the active draft, implement a replace-record operation with unsaved-edit handling, or use a stable record-based identity when a record switch should create a fresh editor. A random UUID on every render repeatedly destroys local state and explains the erased typing. Test that an unrelated parent change preserves edits, that switching records follows the chosen confirmation or reset rule, and that explicit Reset behaves independently. Keep model initialization free of required side effects because description construction can create candidate instances without replacing existing storage. Persistence remains a separate requirement.
followUps: How would the policy differ for an editor that must keep drafts for multiple records?
Why is resetting identity different from mutating the current draft's fields?
pitfalls: Expecting every new initializer argument to overwrite existing State.
Using random identity to force updates without considering state destruction.

questions.prompt: Describe creation, updates, callback coordination, and teardown for a dynamic UIKit representable inside SwiftUI.
questions.scenario: A synthetic UIKitMessage receives changing message text and an onEdit closure. Its represented controller should keep its identity, while its delegate must call the latest callback rather than the first wrapper's callback.
questions.androidBridge: Compose AndroidView's factory and update responsibilities resemble a representable's make and update methods. SwiftUI's representable Coordinator has framework-specific lifetime and delegate duties; it is not automatically a navigation coordinator, Fragment, or coroutine scope.
rubric: Creates the controller in make and applies changing input in update.
Keeps delegate integration on a stable coordinator.
Refreshes the coordinator's current callback or binding during updates.
Teardown cancels only bridge-owned work and avoids redundant user-edit events.
questions.answerHTML:
makeUIViewController creates the UIKit controller for the represented identity. updateUIViewController applies current SwiftUI inputs to that existing instance, so changing text should not require recreating the controller. If updating a label requires the hierarchy, the controller can load it deliberately before assignment.

The representable's coordinator carries delegate and callback integration across temporary wrapper values. Update its current closure or binding when inputs change; retaining the initial wrapper forever can deliver edits to obsolete state. Compare existing and incoming text before assignment when unnecessary writes would disturb selection or focus, and avoid treating a state synchronization as a new user edit. Teardown can detach delegates and cancel subscriptions owned by this bridge, with an explicit lifetime policy. It must not cancel a shared operation merely because one wrapper disappears. The representable coordinator solves interoperability lifetime, while navigation ownership and hosted-controller containment remain separate decisions.
followUps: When is an empty update method appropriate?
Which observation would distinguish a stale callback from a stale controller label?
pitfalls: Recreating the controller for every input update.
Keeping the coordinator's first closure even after its destination changes.

questions.prompt: Audit every exit from a mixed UIKit–SwiftUI picker and explain why search-no-results and invalid initial input have different completion behavior.
questions.scenario: A synthetic picker can select, cancel, be popped by back navigation, be swiped away as a modal, or show no search matches. It also has optional lookup work and a weak presentation delegate. An empty initial data set violates its invocation contract.
questions.androidBridge: Android navigation results and dialog dismissal callbacks raise similar finish-once and cleanup questions. UIKit pushed removal and presentation-controller delegation are distinct paths; Swift weak delegate storage does not supply the delegate adapter's lifetime, unlike assuming callback registration retains an Android listener.
rubric: Maps selection to a selected result and terminal user exits to cancellation.
Keeps search-no-results active rather than finishing the flow.
Treats invalid initial input as invocation recovery rather than ordinary empty success.
Names delegate retention, finish-once protection, and per-path lookup cleanup.
questions.answerHTML:
Build an outcome table before changing navigation. Selection returns the selected value; explicit Cancel, pushed removal, and interactive modal dismissal end with cancellation. Search-no-results keeps the picker active so the user can change the query. Invalid initial input violates this picker's contract and follows its diagnostic and alert recovery path, rather than representing a completed search with zero matches.

Each terminal path must identify who delivers the result and stops optional lookup work. Retain the dismissal adapter elsewhere because a weak delegate reference cannot keep it alive. Disable competing removal callbacks during an explicit selected-result transition and preserve the finish-once caller contract even if result storage rejects duplicates. The lesson identifies different lookup-cleanup paths in source; that is a concrete review question, not observed runtime harm. Verify with controlled pending work and focused navigation integration checks. A direct delegate invocation establishes callback handling but does not prove an actual swipe gesture completed.
followUps: What could make a first-result guard insufficient as a cleanup strategy?
How would you test a lookup that completes after pushed removal?
pitfalls: Finishing cancellation whenever a search returns no matches.
Assuming assignment to a weak delegate keeps its adapter alive.

questions.prompt: Explain why a MainActor loading model still needs revision checks after await and in its error path.
questions.scenario: Synthetic request A suspends, B starts and completes, then A either succeeds or fails. The model publishes loading, loaded, failed, or idle; cancellation of the latest request uses the documented idle policy.
questions.androidBridge: Kotlin suspend functions also suspend without inherently selecting a background dispatcher. MainActor resembles a declared UI isolation domain, while Dispatchers.Main familiarity does not imply atomicity across suspension. A canceled coroutine or Swift task can require cooperative checks and a separate freshness policy.
rubric: Describes await as suspension and possible interleaving rather than automatic background execution.
Captures a request revision before waiting.
Validates freshness before success and failure publication.
Separates cancellation classification from an ordinary service failure and chosen UI policy.
questions.answerHTML:
MainActor isolates accesses to UI state, but an async method can suspend and let another operation change that state. Capture the current request revision when starting the load. After awaiting the service, check cancellation and confirm the captured revision still matches before assigning loaded. That protects against a service that finishes despite a cancellation request.

Perform the same freshness comparison in the catch path. Otherwise A's late error or cancellation can replace B's newer loaded result with failed or idle. Only the current request may apply the model's cancellation policy; this example chooses idle, while another feature could retain earlier content. Classify cancellation using the task state and the service's documented cancellation behavior rather than assuming every API throws the same error type. The async keyword does not guarantee off-main work, and actor isolation does not preserve pre-await assumptions. Use controlled A/B completions to verify both late success and late failure.
followUps: How would retaining previous content change the latest-cancellation policy?
Why does checking cancellation only before the service call leave a gap?
pitfalls: Treating MainActor as an atomic lock across the whole async method.
Guarding stale success while allowing stale failure to clear current UI state.

questions.prompt: Find the lifetime break in a view task that launches another Task, and explain why dropping its handle or adding weak self does not define cancellation.
questions.scenario: A synthetic SwiftUI screen uses .task(id: query) { Task { await model.load(id: query) } }. Rapid query changes leave older operations running, and disappearance sometimes produces an unavailable message.
questions.androidBridge: Compose LaunchedEffect(key) is a useful conceptual neighbor of .task(id:), but creating independently owned coroutine work can also escape the expected scope. Swift Task braces create unstructured work; lexical nesting does not make it a coroutineScope-style structured child.
rubric: Identifies the nested Task as separately owned unstructured work.
Calls the async model directly from the framework-associated task.
Explains cooperative cancellation and why dropping a handle does not cancel.
Retains freshness checks and explicit cancellation-to-UI mapping.
questions.answerHTML:
The outer modifier provides view-associated work and requests cancellation when its ID changes or its lifetime ends. The inner Task creates a separate unstructured task; it does not become a managed child merely because its code is nested there. Await the model's async operation directly inside the modifier so that it executes in the associated task instead.

If a synchronous event legitimately launches unstructured work, assign a feature owner, retain its handle, and cancel it at the defined stopping event. Dropping the handle is not cancellation, and weak capture only changes object ownership. Cancellation remains cooperative: check it after suspension and avoid mapping it to an ordinary unavailable error. Keep request revisions because old work may finish before or despite cancellation. Verify replacement and disappearance with a controlled service, including an old error after a new success. This reasoning defines a task and presentation contract, without asserting that a real transport stopped on a device.
followUps: When would work intentionally outlive the view and require another owner?
What should happen if the fake ignores cancellation but eventually returns?
pitfalls: Assuming a nested Task inherits structured lifetime from the outer task.
Using weak self as a substitute for cancellation and freshness checks.

questions.prompt: Design deterministic cancellation and stale-response tests, distinguishing pre-cancelled work from cancellation after the service has started.
questions.scenario: A synthetic loading model has an injectable async service. The existing test cancels immediately after creating a Task. A proposed overlapping-request test waits ten milliseconds before starting B.
questions.androidBridge: Kotlin coroutine test schedulers and controlled fakes help establish ordering rather than wall-clock luck. Swift Task.yield and sleep are not equivalents of runTest's scheduling controls; XCTest expectations or explicit async signals must encode the event you need to observe.
rubric: Explains the limited pre-cancelled behavior covered by immediate cancellation.
Waits for a fake start signal before cancellation or replacement.
Controls B-before-A completion and repeats with an old failure.
Awaits owned task completion and cleans up every pending fake operation.
questions.answerHTML:
Immediate cancellation can verify the pre-cancelled path, but it does not prove that cancellation occurred while a service was waiting. Give the fake an explicit start signal and a completion gate. Start the operation, await that signal, request cancellation, release the fake, await the owning task's completion, and assert the documented state. This still works when the fake deliberately ignores cancellation.

For freshness, start A and observe its gate, then start B and observe B's gate. Complete B and establish its loaded result before completing A. Assert that A's late success cannot overwrite B; repeat with A failing to check the catch guard. A sleep or yield cannot establish these events reliably. Use the appropriate actor isolation for the model and asynchronous XCTest fulfillment when callback evidence is needed. Ensure every gate is released and every task is joined so no work mutates state after the assertion or hangs the test.
followUps: How would the test fail if only the catch freshness guard were removed?
Why can a blocking wait on MainActor prevent its own fulfillment?
pitfalls: Using a longer sleep to make a scheduling assumption appear reliable.
Leaving gated fake work pending after the test's assertions.

questions.prompt: Evaluate a snapshot diff after an environment change and explain which additional evidence is needed for terminal results and real interaction.
questions.scenario: A synthetic picker snapshot changes after a toolchain update. One teammate proposes recording all baselines. Another claims the unchanged UI identifier and a direct modal-dismissal delegate test prove accessibility and swipe behavior.
questions.androidBridge: Android screenshot tests and Espresso-style interaction checks also answer different questions. SnapshotTesting is a third-party iOS library, while XCUIApplication operates across an app boundary; neither is a direct substitute for model assertions or a complete TalkBack or VoiceOver task review.
rubric: Inspects baseline, candidate, fixtures, fonts, OS, and rendering conditions before recording.
Keeps snapshot rendering evidence distinct from coordinator result assertions.
Distinguishes direct callback tests from actual gesture integration.
Explains why a test identifier cannot establish spoken accessibility quality.
questions.answerHTML:
Inspect the old and new images and identify whether the change is intended behavior or altered rendering conditions. Check the fixture state, registered fonts, layout timing, dimensions, appearance, scale, OS, and SDK. Recording is a reviewed baseline update, not a universal repair for a failing assertion. Increasing tolerance can hide a regression, so justify its meaning.

A snapshot establishes a visual contract under those conditions. A coordinator test establishes the selected or cancelled result, while a focused UI test can verify app-level navigation and an actual gesture. Invoking the presentation delegate directly checks callback integration but does not perform UIKit's swipe transition. A stable accessibility identifier supports automation lookup; it does not establish labels, focus order, or task completion with VoiceOver. Choose the narrow additional evidence for the changed requirement, and label unexecuted checks as planned. One phone-size snapshot cannot establish large-text, localization, or tablet behavior.
followUps: Which changes justify adding a large-text snapshot rather than only updating the default one?
How would you make the app deterministic for an XCUIApplication test?
pitfalls: Re-recording every snapshot to make the suite green.
Claiming an identifier or direct delegate call proves the full user interaction.

questions.prompt: Sketch the draft model and ownership wiring for the booking lab, explaining validation, selection, review, and Reset as one coherent behavior contract.
questions.scenario: A synthetic app collects displayName and optional reason, presents a reason picker, pushes Review, embeds UIKitMessage, and loads a synthetic review result. Returning from Review should preserve edits; Reset clears the fields without replacing navigation.
questions.androidBridge: One hoisted Compose state holder or Android UI-state owner resembles this shared draft boundary. SwiftUI Observation and identity-associated State have different mechanics from StateFlow or ViewModel; a modal NavigationStack is a separate presentation scope rather than a second copy of the draft.
rubric: Defines one MainActor observable draft with optional selection and derived canReview.
Rejects whitespace-only names without maintaining a separate validity flag.
Shares the same root-owned model with picker and review.
Separates explicit field reset, navigation state, UIKit updates, and review-task lifetime.
questions.answerHTML:
Create one MainActor observable draft with a display name, optional reason, computed canReview, and reset(). Compute eligibility from a trimmed nonempty name and a present reason instead of keeping a second mutable validity flag. The root owns the model in State, and picker and review receive that same reference. Editing controls need binding projections; read-only summaries and selection buttons can use ordinary observable reads and assignments.

A selection writes the chosen reason and dismisses the picker. Cancel only dismisses, preserving any existing choice. Review navigation leaves the root owner intact, so returning keeps the draft. Reset clears fields explicitly without randomly changing identity or replacing the stack. Apply current review text through the UIKit bridge's update method and give the synthetic load a view-associated task. Validate fields with model tests, then check picker cancellation, navigation return, bridge sizing, and task behavior at their actual integration boundaries.
followUps: What should choosing the same reason twice do?
Why should Reset not be implemented by assigning a random root identity?
pitfalls: Copying independent drafts into picker and review.
Treating validity, presentation, and navigation as unrelated mutable flags that cannot conflict.

questions.prompt: Trace two lab regressions to the responsible boundaries: Cancel changes a previous reason, and the UIKit review message remains old after the draft changes.
questions.scenario: A synthetic picker writes each highlighted row directly into the committed draft before confirmation. Its Cancel only dismisses. Review reads the shared model correctly, but UIKitMessage has an empty updateUIViewController method.
questions.androidBridge: Android dialogs with provisional state can also corrupt committed selections if they write too early. Compose AndroidView updates offer a similar bridge checkpoint, but SwiftUI representable updates and scoped dismissal follow their own lifecycle; reactive model observation alone does not update a UIKit label.
rubric: Identifies provisional highlight being committed before the cancellation decision.
Chooses immediate selection or a local draft with explicit confirm as a consistent policy.
Applies current message through updateUIViewController.
Tests cancel with an existing selection and dynamic updates on the same controller identity.
questions.answerHTML:
Cancel cannot undo a change that the picker already committed unless the contract explicitly supports restoration. Choose one interaction model: immediate row selection commits and dismisses, as in the lab, or provisional local selection commits only on Confirm. Under the second model, Cancel discards local state and preserves the root draft's previous reason. Test cancellation both with no selection and with an existing one.

The stale UIKit message has a different cause. Observation can cause SwiftUI to recompute the wrapper, but an empty update method never applies the new input to its retained controller. Implement update to call the controller's display method with the current message, loading its hierarchy if necessary. Verify that the same controller identity displays the changed value. Record model events, presentation changes, and bridge updates separately to establish the causal chain. Random identity resets could hide both symptoms while destroying the draft, so they do not satisfy the stated contract.
followUps: Which event log would prove that Cancel preserved the committed reason?
What would you inspect if the message updates correctly but its row has zero height?
pitfalls: Writing tentative row highlights into committed state before deciding cancellation semantics.
Assuming observable reads automatically configure an embedded UIKit view.

questions.prompt: Describe an evidence-backed feature trace from one user action through composition, state, rendering, navigation, and result delivery.
questions.scenario: You review the course's visit-reason picker walkthrough and compare it with the address form. You can inspect lesson-linked source and tests, but have no retained app run or device observations.
questions.androidBridge: Tracing an Android feature through navigation, ViewModel, repository, and tests provides a useful investigation habit. Swift coordinators, hosted-controller containment, weak delegates, and Observation differ in ownership; a familiar architecture name cannot replace checking the actual iOS integration contract.
rubric: Begins with the public input, output, presentation, and caller obligations.
Maps data responsibilities separately from strong and weak ownership.
Follows query changes, selection callbacks, and terminal result delivery.
Labels source facts, conditional risks, planned checks, and actual execution evidence.
questions.answerHTML:
Begin at the public contract: valid input, selected or cancelled output, allowed presentation styles, isolation, and the caller's lifetime obligations. Follow the entry wrapper into its UIKit host, retained coordinator, observable model, hosted view, delegate callback, and result delivery. Separately mark strong owners and weak references; a dependency arrow is not automatically a retaining edge.

Trace a query edit into derived rows, then selection through the model delegate into the navigation transition and finish call. Include back removal, modal dismissal, invalid input, and nonterminal no matches. Compare the address form's caller-owned hosted containment rather than assuming the same coordinator owns everything. Map model, coordinator, snapshot, and UI tests to the requirements they express. Source and test inspection support facts about declarations and intended coverage, not executed results. Write conditional risks with their assumptions and name the check that would resolve them. This produces a review another engineer can verify without claiming a device run.
followUps: Why can a weak hosting-controller property coexist with a visible retained screen?
How would you distinguish a public finish-once promise from defensive duplicate-result protection?
pitfalls: Starting from internal property wrappers and missing the caller contract.
Reporting test source as successful runtime coverage.

questions.prompt: Review the lesson's cleanup asymmetry between explicit pop and pushed removal, then propose the smallest test that can establish its consequence.
questions.scenario: The lesson traces explicit pop through fetchTask.cancel() before finish, while pushed removal calls finish(.cancelled) directly. The base finish delivers the first result but does not cancel subclass task properties. No harmful runtime behavior has been observed.
questions.androidBridge: Android navigation result completion does not necessarily cancel a separately launched coroutine either. Swift's coordinator finish and unstructured Task ownership are distinct contracts; first-result protection is not a LifecycleScope-style automatic cleanup mechanism.
rubric: States the source-observed difference without declaring a proven leak or user-visible defect.
Defines whether every terminal path should cancel optional lookup work.
Uses a fake start signal and controlled late completion after pushed removal.
Checks result count, update policy, and remaining work at the relevant boundary.
questions.answerHTML:
The source trace establishes a cleanup difference: explicit pop requests fetch cancellation, while pushed removal delivers cancellation directly. Because base finish does not manage subclass task properties, its first-result guard does not supply the missing cleanup policy. This supports a focused question about intended lifetime, not a demonstrated leak or harmful update.

Define whether optional suggestions should stop on every terminal path. Use a fake lookup that signals start and waits behind a gate. Start the flow, wait for that signal, trigger the pushed-removal path, then inspect cancellation state and release the lookup with success or failure. Assert the agreed no-update behavior, exactly one cancelled result, and eventual work cleanup. A helper-level test can isolate callbacks; a focused UI path is needed if actual gesture and container integration are the uncertain part. Explain any remaining ownership that keeps the model alive and report the test as planned until it executes.
followUps: What if finish safely rejects a second result but optional work still runs?
Which separate check would prove actual interactive navigation removal?
pitfalls: Calling a source asymmetry a confirmed production incident.
Assuming finish automatically cancels every task retained by a subclass.

questions.prompt: Compare async let with a bounded throwing task group, explaining result order, mutation ownership, and all-or-nothing failure.
questions.scenario: A synthetic dashboard has two independent fixed loads. Another operation loads a variable array of IDs, must preserve input order, and permits at most three in-flight loads without publishing a partial array.
questions.androidBridge: Kotlin coroutineScope with async children resembles structured Swift async let and task-group ownership. Swift task groups yield completion order and are not a direct supervisorScope counterpart; catching child failures deliberately changes whether partial success is allowed.
rubric: Chooses async let for a fixed independent pair and a group for dynamic work.
Tags child results with input indices and mutates output only in the parent.
Seeds three children and adds one replacement per completion.
Explains cancellation and joining when an error escapes the group body.
questions.answerHTML:
Use async let for the fixed dashboard pair, then await both results when constructing the dashboard. For a dynamic list, use a scoped throwing task group whose children return an index and immutable value. Group results arrive in completion order, so the parent stores each value at its original index. Children should not concurrently mutate the parent's output array.

Seed at most three children and submit one new input after each completion frees a slot. Empty input starts none. If an error escapes the group body, remaining children are cancelled and joined, and the function throws instead of returning a partial array. Catching each child into Result would intentionally define another policy. Structured scope exit waits for its children; cancellation is cooperative rather than forced termination. The window bounds active loads, not total result memory or requests per second. Verify ordering, peak activity, failure, and cancellation with explicit fake gates.
followUps: Why can a concurrency limit of three still violate a requests-per-second budget?
How would a partial-success contract change the result type and error handling?
pitfalls: Returning task-group completion order as if it were input order.
Submitting every input at once and calling that a bounded loader.

questions.prompt: Explain why racing an operation against a timeout in a task group can still return late, and define the missing cooperation and ownership contracts.
questions.scenario: A synthetic operation wraps a callback source in a checked continuation. A timeout child wins and cancels siblings, but the callback source ignores cancellation. The caller expects the group to return immediately at the deadline.
questions.androidBridge: Kotlin withTimeout also relies on cooperation and cannot forcibly terminate arbitrary blocking work. Swift group scope additionally joins its children; CheckedContinuation is a one-result bridge, not an automatic cancellation-aware replacement for suspendCancellableCoroutine.
rubric: Explains group scope waiting for cancelled children to finish.
Distinguishes deadline selection from forced termination of the underlying source.
Requires cancellation integration and exactly-once continuation completion under races.
Uses gated cancellation-versus-completion tests and states any remaining timeout limitation.
questions.answerHTML:
The timeout wins the race but does not force the other child to finish. Leaving the task-group scope waits for children, including those that were cancelled. A callback operation that ignores cancellation can therefore keep the group waiting after the nominal deadline. The timeout selection and a transport's own timeout are different mechanisms.

Define how the bridge cancels its underlying operation and how the continuation completes when cancellation races a normal callback. A checked continuation must resume exactly once; a cancellation handler may run concurrently, so protect the completion state with a suitable synchronized mechanism rather than an unsafely shared Boolean. If the source cannot be stopped, the design must state that limitation and assign an owner to any work that continues independently. Test completion-before-cancellation and cancellation-before-completion using gates, then join every task. Do not recover by swallowing cancellation into an empty success or by promising a hard deadline that the dependency cannot honor.
followUps: What cleanup can defer perform if asynchronous cleanup is required?
When would a transport-level timeout provide stronger evidence than a task-group race?
pitfalls: Assuming cancelAll forcibly stops a callback operation.
Resuming a continuation from both cancellation and completion without synchronization.

questions.prompt: Explain actor reentrancy using a reset during a suspended load, including what happens to both the cache and the waiting caller.
questions.scenario: A synthetic SnapshotStore actor starts loading, then reset increments a generation and clears cached data. The loader ignores cancellation and later returns. The contract rejects old-account success rather than merely refusing cache insertion.
questions.androidBridge: An actor serializes isolated state access, whereas a Kotlin Mutex held across a suspend call can exclude other holders for the whole critical section. Swift actor methods permit interleaving at suspension; neither actors nor mutexes alone define account ownership, caller outcomes, or distributed transactions.
rubric: Identifies reset as legal interleaving while load is suspended.
Captures generation before waiting and checks it after cancellation handling.
Rejects stale success for the waiting caller as well as preventing insertion.
States that same-generation concurrent loads need a separate latest-request or coalescing policy.
questions.answerHTML:
The actor protects mutable state from unsynchronized access, but it does not lock the entire async method across the loader's await. Reset can run during that suspension. Capture the account generation before waiting, check cancellation after the loader returns, then compare the generation before the synchronous cache commit. A mismatch throws the documented account-changed outcome and leaves the cache empty.

This store rejects old success for the waiting caller too. A generalized cache might instead return an old result while refusing insertion; that is a different contract that must not be copied accidentally. Cancellation reduces wasted work, while generation validation preserves correctness even if the loader ignores it. Two concurrent loads in the same generation can still finish in either order, so this simple store does not establish latest-request-wins or coalescing. Add those policies explicitly when callers need them. Actor safety also does not override a disk framework's confinement rules or establish a transaction with a server.
followUps: Why does matching the account string after A-to-B-to-A not establish current ownership?
How would you test the waiting caller's outcome separately from cached state?
pitfalls: Calling actor data-race safety a transaction across await.
Checking only that stale data was not cached while returning it as current account success.

questions.prompt: Evaluate a proposed Sendable conformance and nonisolated escape hatch for a snapshot containing a mutable class.
questions.scenario: A synthetic struct holds let notes: MutableNotes and is passed between tasks. To quiet compiler diagnostics, a teammate adds @unchecked Sendable and makes an actor accessor nonisolated while reading mutable actor state.
questions.androidBridge: Kotlin val holding a mutable object does not make that object immutable or thread-safe, just as Swift let does not. Kotlin has no exact compiler-enforced Sendable counterpart; mutex or dispatcher conventions cannot justify a Swift unchecked annotation without a documented synchronization invariant.
rubric: Identifies the mutable nested reference despite the outer value type and let field.
Separates Sendable values from @Sendable closure capture constraints.
Explains that unchecked conformance adds no synchronization.
Rejects nonisolated access to mutable actor state and proposes safe snapshots or an owner.
questions.answerHTML:
The struct's value semantics do not make its referenced MutableNotes safe to transfer. The let property freezes which reference is stored, not the object's mutable text. Prefer an immutable snapshot containing Sendable value fields, or keep mutable notes under an actor and access them through its isolation contract. Actors can be safely referenced across domains because their isolated members remain controlled.

Sendable describes transfer safety of values; @Sendable constrains closure captures and their use. @unchecked Sendable is a manual promise and adds no lock, so it needs a complete documented protection mechanism that the compiler cannot establish. Marking an accessor nonisolated opts it out of actor isolation; it cannot thereby safely read arbitrary mutable isolated state. Return a snapshot through an isolated operation instead. Likewise, referencing a MainActor model from another domain does not permit synchronous mutation of its UI properties. Diagnose the ownership and access invariant rather than suppressing the diagnostic.
followUps: What captured test counter would make an @Sendable fake unsafe?
When could a genuinely immutable property support a nonisolated API?
pitfalls: Assuming let means deep immutability and automatic Sendable safety.
Using unchecked or nonisolated as synchronization mechanisms.

questions.prompt: Explain what a newest-one AsyncStream buffer guarantees for progress, and why the same policy can corrupt required event deltas.
questions.scenario: A synthetic callback producer emits progress faster than one consumer processes it. The stream uses bufferingNewest(1). Another team wants to reuse that factory for ordered text fragments and assumes slow iteration suspends production.
questions.androidBridge: Kotlin Flow, StateFlow, and channels help distinguish collection, replaceable state, and required events. AsyncSequence does not imply cold Flow behavior or multicast, and continuation-based AsyncStream.yield does not suspend the producer like a suspending channel send.
rubric: Describes one newest waiting element and possible dropped older buffered values.
Separates bounded buffering from producer backpressure.
Permits replacement for progress but rejects loss of dependent deltas.
Defines single-consumer, producer start, termination, and payload-size limits.
questions.answerHTML:
bufferingNewest(1) keeps the newest waiting element and can drop older buffered progress. That is acceptable when each value is a complete replaceable state and the contract allows skipping intermediate progress. It does not make the producer wait for the consumer: continuation yield returns an enqueue, drop, or termination result instead of suspending until space exists.

Ordered text fragments may depend on every earlier fragment, so dropping them can corrupt the output. Use complete cumulative snapshots or a producer-consumer protocol that explicitly provides backpressure and required-event handling. A one-element bound also does not bound bytes if an element can be enormous. Define production start time, consumer count, overflow, failure, and stopping behavior. Constructing a stream can start its producer before iteration, and one AsyncStream is not automatically a broadcast channel. Observe yield results when loss matters and provide explicit early-stop behavior rather than assuming a loop break cancels every retained producer.
followUps: How does bufferingOldest(1) differ for a burst of progress?
What additional bound is needed if each state contains a large payload?
pitfalls: Calling a buffer limit backpressure.
Using newest-only buffering for required ordered event fragments.

questions.prompt: Audit a reactive-to-async bridge that hides upstream failure and a reverse bridge that starts producing before subscription.
questions.scenario: A synthetic publisher adapter finishes AsyncStream normally on failure. Its reverse adapter starts a Task feeding a PassthroughSubject before returning the publisher, and subscriber cancellation has no connection to the task handle.
questions.androidBridge: Converting RxJava or Kotlin Flow sources can likewise change errors, replay, start timing, and disposal. Combine demand and subject semantics differ from Flow collection, and Swift async iteration does not automatically preserve either library's failure or cancellation contract.
rubric: Identifies failure-to-normal-completion as an observable semantic change.
Identifies possible loss before subscribers attach.
Connects subscriber or iterator termination to bridge-owned producer cleanup.
Tests timing, failure, buffering, and cancellation rather than only emitted happy-path values.
questions.answerHTML:
The first adapter turns failure into ordinary end-of-sequence. That can be valid for best-effort notifications, but a data consumer expecting an error loses its recovery signal. Use a throwing sequence when failure belongs to the contract, or explicitly document the intended loss. Test failure separately from normal completion.

The reverse adapter starts work before subscription, so a nonreplaying subject can miss early values. It also lacks a defined stop path if subscriber cancellation never reaches the producing task. Choose subscription-driven start or deliberate replay according to the source, and assign ownership of the producer handle. For the async side, connect termination to cleanup and provide an explicit stop when an early consumer exit otherwise retains the source. Verify creation without consumption, late subscription, early stop, and completion races with controlled fixtures. These are adapter risks supported by their structure; whether any caller experiences harm still requires tracing its assumptions and observing the relevant path.
followUps: When would normal completion on failure be an acceptable intentional contract?
Why does canceling a subscription not inherently cancel an independently created Task?
pitfalls: Calling the bridge equivalent because its return type looks similar.
Declaring a production incident without checking callers and schedules.

questions.prompt: Explain HTTP validation before decoding and the difference between an optional read field and a three-way patch field.
